title: 01 — How Generative AI Works
html:
01 — How Generative AI Works

The one idea: a language model reads text as tokens and repeatedly predicts the next one. Everything you control (the instructions, the documents you include, the tools you offer, the sampling settings) works by changing what it sees before it predicts.

1. What it is

Term Meaning
Token A chunk of text (a word, part of a word, punctuation). Models read and write tokens, and you pay per token
Tokenizer The fixed rule that splits text into tokens. Most use byte-pair encoding (BPE) or a close relative
Context window The maximum tokens a model can consider at once (input plus output). Current frontier models offer up to about 1 million tokens
Next-token prediction The model outputs a probability for every possible next token. Generation repeats this one token at a time
Temperature, sampling How the next token is picked from those probabilities. Some newer models fix sampling and remove these settings
Embedding A vector that represents meaning. It powers search, clustering and retrieval
Pre-training, instruction tuning, RLHF Learning language from huge text, then learning to follow instructions, then learning preferred behaviour from feedback
Reasoning, thinking Models that spend extra tokens working through a problem before answering. More effort usually means better answers, at more cost and latency
Multimodal Models that also read images, PDFs or audio, or produce them

2. Why it matters

  • Cost and limits are in tokens. Long system prompts, chat history and documents all count on every request.
  • The model only knows what is in its weights (frozen at training time) and its context. Current or private facts must be supplied, through retrieval or tools.
  • Outputs are probabilistic. The same question can produce different wording, so you evaluate on sets of cases, not single examples (08).

3. The main ideas

3.1 From text to text

---
title: What happens on one model call
---
flowchart LR
    IN["System prompt + history + documents + tools + question"] --> TOK["Tokenizer"]
    TOK --> M["Model: predict next-token<br/>probabilities"]
    M --> S["Pick a token<br/>(sampling)"]
    S --> APP["Append, repeat until a stop"]
    APP --> OUT["Text, a tool call, or structured JSON"]
    APP -. "loop" .-> M

3.2 Model families and how to choose

Family Examples (2026) Strengths Trade-offs
Frontier, hosted Claude (Opus, Sonnet, Haiku tiers), GPT, Gemini Best reasoning, tool use, long context Data leaves your perimeter (check terms and region options), per-token cost
Open-weight, self-hosted Llama, Qwen, Gemma, Mistral and others Runs in your perimeter, fine-tunable You run GPUs and serving, and quality varies by task
Specialised Embedding models, rerankers, speech-to-text, text-to-speech, OCR and vision models Cheap and fast at one job One job each

How to choose:

  1. Start with the most capable model on a small evaluation set.
  2. Step down a tier, or lower the reasoning effort, only when measurement shows quality holds.
  3. Judge cost per completed task, not per request.

For Claude, the API documentation lists current model ids and prices. The most capable widely released model is Claude Fable 5.1 (claude-fable-5-1), the default Opus-tier model is Claude Opus 5.5 (claude-opus-5-5), and there are faster, cheaper Sonnet and Haiku tiers (claude-sonnet-5-5, claude-haiku-5-5). Always use exact ids from the docs.

3.3 Grounding: how private or current knowledge gets in

Need Technique Note
Facts from your documents Retrieval (RAG): search, then include passages with sources LLM Engineering & RAG, hybrid search
Live data or actions Tools and function calling 02, 04
A style, format or narrow skill Prompting first, then fine-tuning Fine-Tuning and LoRA

4. Working code

The script trains a tiny BPE tokenizer on a sentence, then shows how temperature changes next-token sampling. Standard library only.

import math, random
from collections import Counter

# 1. Byte-pair encoding (BPE), the idea behind most LLM tokenizers: start from characters and
#    repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token.
corpus = "net asset value rose . net asset value fell . net inflows rose . asset allocation"
words = [list(w) + ["</w>"] for w in corpus.split()]
merges = []
for _ in range(10):
    pairs = Counter((a, b) for w in words for a, b in zip(w, w[1:]))
    if not pairs:
        break
    (a, b), count = pairs.most_common(1)[0]
    merges.append(a + b)
    new_words = []
    for w in words:
        out, i = [], 0
        while i < len(w):
            if i + 1 < len(w) and w[i] == a and w[i + 1] == b:
                out.append(a + b); i += 2
            else:
                out.append(w[i]); i += 1
        new_words.append(out)
    words = new_words
print("first merges learned:", merges[:6])
print("'net asset value' is now:", words[0] + words[1] + words[2])

# 2. Next-token sampling: the model outputs a score (logit) per candidate token.
#    Temperature reshapes the distribution before sampling. Low = predictable, high = varied.
logits = {"rose": 2.0, "fell": 1.6, "was": 0.9, "banana": -2.0}
def softmax(logits, temperature):
    exps = {t: math.exp(v / temperature) for t, v in logits.items()}
    total = sum(exps.values())
    return {t: e / total for t, e in exps.items()}
random.seed(3)
for temp in (0.2, 1.0, 2.0):
    probs = softmax(logits, temp)
    draws = Counter(random.choices(list(probs), weights=list(probs.values()), k=1000))
    print(f"temperature {temp}: " + ", ".join(f"{t} {probs[t]:.2f}" for t in logits) +
          f" | 1000 samples: {dict(draws.most_common())}")

Output:

first merges learned: ['et', 'et</w>', 'e</w>', 'net</w>', 'as', 'ass']
'net asset value' is now: ['net</w>', 'asset</w>', 'val', 'u', 'e</w>']
temperature 0.2: rose 0.88, fell 0.12, was 0.00, banana 0.00 | 1000 samples: {'rose': 877, 'fell': 120, 'was': 3}
temperature 1.0: rose 0.49, fell 0.33, was 0.16, banana 0.01 | 1000 samples: {'rose': 498, 'fell': 321, 'was': 172, 'banana': 9}
temperature 2.0: rose 0.40, fell 0.32, was 0.23, banana 0.05 | 1000 samples: {'rose': 394, 'fell': 324, 'was': 228, 'banana': 54}

What to notice:

  • Frequent pieces become single tokens. After ten merges, "net" and "asset" are one token each, while the rarer "value" is still split into three. Real tokenizers learn tens of thousands of merges from huge corpora, which is why common words are cheap and rare ones cost several tokens.
  • At temperature 0.2 the top token dominates (877 of 1000 draws). At 2.0, even "banana" is picked 54 times. Low randomness suits extraction and classification. More randomness suits brainstorming.

5. Common mistakes

  1. Assuming the model knows your data. It knows only its training data and what you put in the context.
  2. Counting words, not tokens. Use the provider's token-counting endpoint for budgets.
  3. Choosing the cheapest model first. Prove quality on the best model, then step down with measurement.
  4. Judging from one example. Outputs vary, so evaluate on a set.
  5. Stuffing everything into the context. Irrelevant text costs money and can distract the model. Retrieve what matters.

6. Exercise (45 minutes)

  1. Run the BPE script for 30 merges, and watch which words become single tokens.
  2. Add a token "fell" with a logit close to "rose", and see how temperature changes which one wins.
  3. Pick one task you would build (for example, classifying support emails). Write which model tier you would start with, and how you'd decide to step down.

7. Questions to test yourself

  1. What is a token, and why does it matter for cost?
  2. Where does a model's knowledge come from?
  3. What does temperature do?
  4. When would you choose an open-weight model over a hosted frontier model?
  5. What are the three ways to give a model knowledge it doesn't have?

Answers

  1. A chunk of text the model reads or writes. Pricing and context limits are counted in tokens.
  2. From its training data (frozen at training time) and from whatever is in its context on each request.
  3. It flattens (higher) or sharpens (lower) the next-token probabilities before sampling.
  4. When data must stay in your perimeter, when you need to fine-tune heavily, or when cost at very high volume favours self-hosting, provided quality holds on your evaluation.
  5. Retrieval of documents, tools for live data or actions, and fine-tuning for behaviour or format.

8. Sources

Checked 2026-10-27.
